composing_text: 3rd Parachute Brigade; 5th Parachute Brigade; 6th Airlanding Brigade; 1st Canadian Parachute Battalion
current_activity: seizing Orne bridges and Caen canal after airborne landing
notes: Landed after 22:56 on 5 June (coup de main on Caen canal and Orne bridges, Merville battery, Dives bridges); entire division fully deployed by 00:00 7 June except 12th Devons (by sea 7 June). [Review 5: strength_json removed. It gave personnel 8,500 (estimate, 'men deployed 5-7 June; about 800 casualties', Wikipedia Operation Tonga, citing Air Ministry). Sources do not agree on what that figure covers: the British Army page calls it 'the 8,500 British and Canadian soldiers of 6th Airborne Division'; the Airborne Assault Museum gives 7,000 for the British paratroopers and glider-borne troops; other histories give about 12,000 for the full division. Pegasus Archive says the two air lifts could not bring the division's full strength and the remainder, including most of the 12th Devons, came by sea on 7 June, but no source says how many men that was or whether 8,500 includes them. Not enough to set whole_unit or sub_force, so no figure is kept; casualties about 800 (Wikipedia Operation Tonga).]

current_activity: relieved at the bridges; holding the Orne bridgehead
notes: 3rd Division relief of airborne troops at the bridges completed ~01:00 on 7 June; division began holding the Orne bridgehead.

current_activity: defending Orne bridgehead and expanding it east
notes: German tanks and infantry made several attacks on the Orne bridgehead on 10 June; 6th Airborne given the task of expanding the bridgehead east of the Orne.

current_activity: attacking Bréville; repulsed with heavy casualties
notes: 5th Black Watch attack on Bréville repulsed 11 June after heavy casualties; German attacks from the Bréville area on 12 June.

current_activity: holding Orne-Dives area until relieved by 51st Highland
notes: Held the area between the Orne and the Dives until 14 June, when 51st Highland Division took over the southern part of the Orne bridgehead.

composing_text: BEL-INF-001B (1st Belgian Infantry Brigade, newly arrived from England and reinforcing the division); NL-INF-IRNEB (Royal Netherlands Brigade, newly arrived from England and reinforcing the division)
current_activity: Reinforced by two commando brigades and the Belgian and Dutch brigades, takes Troarn without difficulty
notes: Event date: by 21 August 1944 (the day is not given) (Ellis, vol. I, p. 448). Event definition: In the coastal sector of I Corps the division, reinforced by the 1st and 4th Special Service Brigades and the 1st Belgian Infantry Brigade and Royal Netherlands Brigade newly arrived from England, takes Troarn without any difficulty; the page places this in the days of the closing of the Falaise Gap (to 21 August) and gives no day, so 21 August is the latest possible date (inferred value); advance across the Dives delta is slow (p. 448). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 448: "In the coastal sector the 6th Airborne Division (reinforced by 1st and 4th Special Service Brigades and Belgian and Dutch contingents newly arrived from England"; "had taken Troarn with- out any difficulty". Location: Troarn, Calvados (place added in the July tranche) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Ellis names Troarn as taken (p. 448).

current_activity: Completes its Normandy task at Pont-Audemer on the Risle; rests on 27 August, never out of the line since 6 June
notes: Event date: 26 August 1944 (Ellis, vol. I, p. 453). Event definition: By early morning on 26 August I Corps holds the line of the Risle from Montfort to the sea, including Pont-Audemer, where the 6th Airborne Division completes its final Normandy task; on 27 August the airborne men rest, the division having never been out of the front line since 6 June (p. 453). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. I, p. 453: "including Pont Audemer where the 6th Airborne Division completed its final Normandy task"; "On the 27th of August the airborne men rested". Location: Pont-Audemer, Eure (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location support: Ellis names Pont Audemer as the place where the division completed its task (p. 453).

current_activity: Ardennes: with the 29th Armoured and 34th Tank Brigades attacks east from east of Givet; hard fight for Bure
notes: Event date: 3 January 1945 (the fight in Bure lasts several days; the page gives 3 January for the start of the attack) (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 190, 191). Event definition: In the XXX Corps attack that begins on 3 January, on the right, the division and the 29th Armoured and 34th Tank Brigades, advancing east from assembly positions east of Givet, have a very hard fight with the Germans in Bure, which changes hands several times in the next few days (pp. 190-191). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, pp. 190-191: "On the right the 6th Airborne Division and the 29th Armoured and 34th Tank Brigades, advancing east from assembly positions east of Givet, had a very hard fight with the Germans in Bure which changed hands several times in the next few days". Location: Bure, Luxembourg province (new place), the village fought for with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is the village of Bure, the place named; the division headquarters is not named and the fight took place in and around the village. Location support: Ellis names Bure as the village fought for (p. 190).

current_activity: Varsity: parachute brigades drop at the Diersfordter Wald and Hamminkeln about 10:00; gliders land by Hamminkeln
notes: Event date: 24 March 1945, about 10:00 (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 290, 291). Event definition: The division is flown in from England as part of the United States XVIII Airborne Corps (with the American 17th Airborne Division) to the Diersfordter Wald, the airborne objective north-west of Wesel: just before ten o'clock the sky fills with parachutes; its two parachute brigades lead in American aircraft, one dropping at the north-west corner of the woods, where some opposition is met but soon overcome, and the other on the north side of the Mehr-Hamminkeln road a mile and a half west of Hamminkeln, where the fire is more intense but the objectives are secured by mid-afternoon; the gliders then land on four zones round Hamminkeln and about half are damaged; six bridges over the Issel are captured intact; by nightfall all organised resistance west of the Issel is overcome, casualties are about 1,400 of 7,220 landed and about 1,500 prisoners are taken (p. 290). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, pp. 290-291: "After they had passed over just before ten o'clock the sky ahead filled with parachutes"; "The British 6th Airborne Division flew in with its two parachute brigades leading in American aircraft, one brigade dropping at the north- west corner of the woods where some opposition was met but soon overcome"; "After the parachutists, the gliders flew in, towed by aircraft of Nos. 38 and 46 Groups, to land on four zones round Hamminkeln"; "By nightfall all organised resistance west of the Issel had been over- come". Location: Hamminkeln, North Rhine-Westphalia (new place), the centre of the four glider landing zones with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is the town of Hamminkeln, the centre of the four glider zones; the parachute brigades dropped at the Diersfordter Wald, about 5 km to the south-west, and the division headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names Hamminkeln, the Diersfordter Wald and the Mehr-Hamminkeln road as the landing and dropping areas (p. 290).

current_activity: Uelzen: by-passes the town to the south with the 11th Armoured Division to the north to hem in the garrison
notes: Event date: 17 April 1945 (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 310, 311). Event definition: While the 15th Division attacks Uelzen, the 6th Airborne and 11th Armoured Divisions, by-passing it to the south and north respectively, endeavour to join hands beyond the town and hem in its garrison, but cannot do so in time to prevent a regimental group of Panzer Division Clausewitz escaping from the trap on the night of 17 April; Uelzen is captured next day (pp. 310-311). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, pp. 310-311: "the 6th Airborne and 11th Armoured Divisions, by-passing it to the south and north respectively, endeavoured to join hands beyond the town and hem in its garrison"; "a regimental group of Panzer Division Clausewitz escaping from the trap on the night of the 17th". Location: Uelzen, Niedersachsen (existing place PL0660), the town by-passed to the south with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the town of Uelzen; the division passed to the south of it and its headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names Uelzen as the town by-passed to the south (p. 310).

current_activity: Baltic: with the US XVIII Airborne Corps takes Wismar; Russian III Tank Corps makes contact that evening
notes: Event date: 2 May 1945 (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 337, 338). Event definition: The division, which started to cross the Elbe on the afternoon of 30 April, joins the United States XVIII Airborne Corps in its bridgehead upstream of VIII Corps; on 2 May the XVIII Airborne Corps quickly secures the line Dömitz-Ludwigslust-Schwerin-Wismar, the last town falling to the 6th Airborne Division, whose leading troops are the 1st Canadian Parachute Battalion riding on the tanks of The Royal Scots Greys; that evening the Russian III Tank Corps makes contact with the division at Wismar, the first British division to land in Normandy on D-day being the first to reach the Baltic and the first to make contact with Soviet forces (pp. 337-338). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 337: "where they were joined by the British 6th Airborne Division"; "the last named town falling to the British 6th Airborne Division"; p. 338: "that evening the Russian III Tank Corps made contact with the 6th Airborne Division at Wismar". Location: Wismar, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern (new place) with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is the town centre of Wismar; the division headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names Wismar as the town taken and the place of contact with the Russians (pp. 337-338).
